To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the spatial variation in the sediment of the Hamilton Harbour (Lake Ontatio, Canada) of potential microbial activities can be explained by the significant environmental factors (NH4+, dissolved organic carbon, particulate carbon, temperature, and dissolved O2) and not much (10–20%) by the spatial structure of the system.

1) most of the observed variation in denitrification, methane, and CO2 production in the sediments of Hamilton Harbour can be explained by environmental factors such as O 2, NO3-, organic carbon, and temperature; 2) denitrification and methane and CO2 production are linked by a carbon cycle in the sediments; 3) denitrification is linked to the organic carbon pool in the sediments.

1) denitrification in Hamilton Harbour sediment is primarily controlled by the availability of NO3− and organic carbon; 2) denitrification is also affected by the spatial structure; and 3) denitrification and methanogenesis are coupled in the sediment of this eutrophic harbour.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a conceptual model of denitrification in Hamilton Harbour sediment.
a systematic sampling approach to study the spatial and temporal variability of potential microbial activities in sediment.

the spatial structure of denitrification in a large urbanized harbour, the importance of the spatial component of denitrification, and the role of the biotic and abiotic factors in explaining the spatial structure of the denitrification capacity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

denitrification and methane formation are closely linked to carbon metabolism, and that the spatial structure of the sediment is a significant factor in determining the potential microbial activities.
denitrification is a process that is strongly controlled by the environmental variables, and to a much less extent, by spatial factors.
the environmental factors are important in explaining the observed variation of microbial activities, but the biotic factor is also significant.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the spatial and environmental components of the variance are important in explaining the variation of potential microbial activities.
the observed variation in denitrification capacity can be explained by a combination of spatial variation (10–30%) and environmental variation (60–90%).

denitrification and methane and CO2 production are related to the availability of organic carbon in the sediment, but that this availability is also dependent on the spatial distribution of the sediment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the spatial structure of the environment is not as important as the abiotic and biotic factors in explaining the observed variation in denitrification and CH4 production.
denitrification is a complex process that is influenced by a number of environmental and spatial factors.

the environmental factors and the spatial structure explain most of the variation of potential microbial activities in the sediment, and that the spatial structure is less important than the environmental factors in explaining variation in the microbial activities.
